title: Write a custom three-argument `@FunctionalInterface TriFunction<A, B, C, R>` with `R apply(A a, B b, C c)` and use it (e.g., sum of three numbers) — explain why Java has no built-in 3-arg function.
shortTitle: Write a custom three-argument @FunctionalInterface TriFunction<A, B, C, R> and explain why Java has no built-in 3-arg function

s1_definition.profdef: Java's `java.util.function` package stops at two arguments (`BiFunction`), so a three-argument function must be a custom `@FunctionalInterface TriFunction<A, B, C, R>` declaring `R apply(A a, B b, C c)`. Java omits a built-in version to avoid a combinatorial explosion of rarely-needed interfaces.
s1_definition.analogy: Priya needs a rule that takes three inputs at once. The standard toolkit only sells one and two-input tools, so she makes her own three-input tool. The toolkit maker stopped at two because almost nobody needs three.
s1_definition.oneliner: Define `TriFunction<A,B,C,R>` yourself — Java caps built-ins at `BiFunction` to prevent interface sprawl.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java's `java.util.function` package stops at two arguments (`BiFunction`), so a three-argument function must be a custom `@FunctionalInterface TriFunction<A, B, C, R>` declaring `R apply(A a, B b, C c)`. Java omits a built-in version to avoid a combinatorial explosion of rarely-needed interfaces.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Priya needs a rule that takes three inputs at once. The standard toolkit only sells one and two-input tools, so she makes her own three-input tool. The toolkit maker stopped at two because almost nobody needs three.

**One line to remember:** Define `TriFunction<A,B,C,R>` yourself — Java caps built-ins at `BiFunction` to prevent interface sprawl.

sections.s2_technical:
You declare `@FunctionalInterface interface TriFunction<A, B, C, R> { R apply(A a, B b, C c); }`, then implement it with a lambda such as `(a, b, c) -> a + b + c`. It is used exactly like Function and BiFunction, just with three inputs: `tri.apply(x, y, z)`.

Java provides Function and BiFunction but no TriFunction because the number of needed combinations grows rapidly — for each arity you would also want primitive specialisations like IntFunction and ToDoubleBiFunction, so three-argument variants would multiply into dozens of interfaces for diminishing benefit. The designers drew the line at two, which covers the overwhelming majority of real cases.

The senior nuance is that when I genuinely need three inputs, I either define a small TriFunction or, often better, introduce a parameter object that bundles the three values and use a normal Function on that object. The parameter-object approach scales to any number of inputs, gives the group a name, and is easier to evolve. Choosing between a TriFunction and a parameter object is a design trade-off between brevity and future growth.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A fee calculation at the National Bank of India depends on three inputs — principal, rate, and tenure — and should be expressed as a single reusable function.

This is exactly what a custom TriFunction does — it takes all three inputs and returns the computed fee, since no built-in three-argument function exists.

The code defines the `TriFunction` interface and a `FeeService` using it.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: principal 1,000,000, rate 8 percent, tenure 3 years.

Step 1: The lambda implements TriFunction's three-argument apply.

Step 2: It multiplies principal by the rate and shifts the decimal two places, giving 80,000 per year.

Step 3: It multiplies by the three-year tenure, giving 240,000.

Step 4: The service returns the computed interest.

```
INFO: Simple interest = 240000.00
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Java's function package stops at two arguments with BiFunction, so when I need a three-argument function I declare my own at FunctionalInterface, TriFunction of A, B, C, and R, with a single apply method taking three inputs. I then implement it with a lambda — for a simple-interest fee at the National Bank of India that is principal, rate, and years to the computed interest — and use it exactly like Function and BiFunction, just with three inputs.

The reason Java has no built-in three-argument function is to avoid a combinatorial explosion. For every arity the library would also want primitive specialisations like IntFunction and ToDoubleBiFunction, so three-argument variants would multiply into dozens of interfaces for very little benefit, and the designers drew the line at two, which covers almost every real case.

The senior point I add is that a TriFunction is not always the best answer. When I need three or more inputs I often introduce a small parameter object that bundles the values and then use an ordinary Function on that object. That approach scales to any number of inputs, gives the group a meaningful name, and is easier to evolve when a fourth input appears. So I weigh a quick TriFunction against a parameter object as a trade-off between brevity now and growth later.
